title: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models
definition: VLAs are foundation models that map visual observations $o_t$ and language instructions $l$ to robot actions $a_t$: $\pi_\theta(a_t | o_t, l)$. They extend VLMs with action prediction heads, trained on large-scale robot demonstration datasets. Architecture: vision encoder (ViT) $\rightarrow$ projection $\rightarrow$ language model backbone $\rightarrow$ action head. Actions often tokenized into discrete bins or predicted as continuous vectors via a diffusion/flow head. Examples: RT-2 ($\pi(a_t | I_t, l) = \text{PaLM-E}(\text{tokenize}(a_t) | I_t, l)$), Octo, OpenVLA.
intuition: A VLM can look at a scene and answer 'what do you see?' A VLA goes further: 'given what you see and the instruction pick up the red cup, what should the robot do?' It bridges language understanding, visual perception, and physical action in one model. Like giving a robot both eyes and a brain that understands natural language commands.
practical_example: RT-2: PaLM-E (VLM) fine-tuned on robot demonstration data. Actions tokenized as text tokens (e.g., 'move_x: 0.05, move_y: -0.02'). Trained on 130K episodes from real robots. Can follow novel instructions by combining language understanding with physical grounding. Octo: smaller open-source VLA trained on Open X-Embodiment dataset, uses a transformer backbone with diffusion action head for multimodal action prediction.
failure_mode: Action space mismatch: VLA trained on one robot's action space (e.g., 7-DOF absolute joint positions) fails on different embodiments. Language grounding failure: model correctly identifies objects but maps to wrong physical actions. Symptoms: correct object identification but wrong grasp approach. Fix: embodiment-specific fine-tuning, action space normalization ($a_{\text{norm}} = (a - \mu_a) / \sigma_a$), add proprioceptive input $q_t$ to the conditioning.
interview_answer: VLAs represent the convergence of foundation models and robotics — one model that sees, understands language, and acts. RT-2 showed that VLMs can be fine-tuned into effective robot policies by tokenizing actions. The key challenges: (1) action space generalization across embodiments (solved partially by datasets like Open X-Embodiment), (2) real-time inference (large models are slow — need distillation or efficient architectures), (3) safety (language understanding doesn't guarantee safe physical behavior). I think VLAs will become the default for high-level task policies, with specialized low-level controllers for precision.

title: Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
definition: Models that jointly process images and text, enabling tasks like visual question answering, image captioning, and visual reasoning. Architecture: vision encoder $f_\text{vis}$ (ViT/CLIP) $\rightarrow$ projection layer $W_p$ $\rightarrow$ language model $f_\text{LM}$. The visual tokens $\mathbf{z} = W_p \cdot f_\text{vis}(I)$ are concatenated with text tokens and processed autoregressively. Examples: GPT-4V, Claude Vision, LLaVA, Gemini. Training: often a two-stage approach — (1) pre-train projection on image-caption pairs, (2) instruction-tune end-to-end.
intuition: A VLM can 'see' and 'talk' about what it sees. Show it a robot workspace photo and ask 'what objects are graspable?' and it can reason about the scene. It's the eyes and reasoning brain, but not the hands — it can plan but not act (that's what VLAs add).
practical_example: Using GPT-4V for robotic task planning: capture workspace image $\rightarrow$ prompt: 'Given this scene, plan the steps to sort objects by color. Output as numbered actions.' $\rightarrow$ parse structured output $\rightarrow$ execute with low-level controller. Works for long-horizon tasks where classical planning fails due to perception complexity.
failure_mode: Spatial reasoning failures: VLMs can identify objects but struggle with precise spatial relationships ('is the cup to the left or right of the bowl?'). Hallucination: confidently describe objects that aren't there. Symptoms: robot reaches for nonexistent objects or wrong locations. Fix: validate VLM outputs with detection/segmentation, use VLMs for high-level planning only (not precise spatial commands).
interview_answer: VLMs bring common-sense reasoning and language understanding to robot perception. The practical pattern: use VLMs for high-level scene understanding and task planning, then hand off to specialized modules for precise spatial reasoning and control. Key insight: VLMs are excellent at semantic understanding ('this is a cluttered kitchen with dishes to clean') but poor at precise spatial reasoning ('the mug handle is 2cm to the left'). In production, I combine VLM-based task planning with classical perception (pose estimation, point clouds) for execution.

title: Language Grounding in Robotics
definition: Connecting natural language to physical actions, objects, and spatial concepts in the real world. Formalized as learning a grounding function $g: \mathcal{L} \times \mathcal{O} \rightarrow \mathcal{E}$ that maps a language expression $l$ and observation $o$ to a grounded entity $e$ (object, region, or action). Includes: referring expression comprehension ('pick up the red cup near the edge'), affordance prediction ('what can I do with this?'), and instruction following ('stack the blocks by color').
intuition: When a human says 'pick up the heavy one,' the robot needs to connect 'heavy' (language) to a physical property it can estimate, identify which object is heaviest, and plan a grasp. Grounding is the bridge between abstract language and concrete physical reality.
practical_example: SayCan (Google): LLM proposes candidate actions in natural language, a learned affordance model $p(\text{feasible} | a, s)$ scores which actions are physically feasible given current state $s$. Combined score: $p(a | l) \cdot p(\text{feasible} | a, s)$ selects the best feasible action. LLM says 'pick up the sponge,' affordance model checks 'is a sponge visible and reachable?' $\rightarrow$ combined score selects the best feasible action.
failure_mode: Grounding failure: language maps to wrong physical entity or impossible action. Example: 'move it closer' — what is 'it'? closer to what? Ambiguity in language + imprecise spatial understanding = wrong action. Fix: explicit disambiguation prompts, maintain dialogue context, use pointing/gaze for reference resolution.
interview_answer: Language grounding connects LLM reasoning to physical robot capabilities. The key frameworks: SayCan (affordance-weighted language planning, scoring $p(a|l) \cdot p(\text{feasible}|a,s)$), Code as Policies (LLM generates Python code for robot APIs), and VLAs (end-to-end language-conditioned policies). The main challenge is the gap between what language describes abstractly and what the robot can physically do. In practice, I advocate for a grounding verification step: after the LLM proposes an action, check it against perception (can I see that object?) and kinematics (can I reach it?) before executing.

title: Visual Representation Learning for Robotics
definition: Learning visual features $\phi(I) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ that are useful for downstream robot tasks, typically through pre-training on large datasets. Methods: contrastive learning (minimize $\mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp(\text{sim}(z_i, z_j)/\tau)}{\sum_k \exp(\text{sim}(z_i, z_k)/\tau)}$ for positive pairs $(i,j)$), masked autoencoders (reconstruct masked patches), self-supervised video prediction. Key: representations should capture task-relevant structure while being invariant to irrelevant visual variation (lighting, background).
intuition: Raw pixels contain too much irrelevant information (shadows, textures, lighting) and not enough task-relevant structure (object pose, contact state). Representation learning compresses images into a feature space where 'similar' means 'similar for the task' — two images of a cup in different lighting should have similar features if the cup is in the same pose.
practical_example: R3M: pre-trained on Ego4D human video data with time-contrastive + language-alignment objectives. Fine-tune a manipulation policy with R3M features instead of raw pixels: $\sim 10\times$ fewer demonstrations needed. DINOv2 features also work well as frozen encoders for manipulation with just a linear probe $\hat{a} = W \phi(I) + b$.
failure_mode: Representation doesn't capture task-relevant features: pre-trained on ImageNet (objects in context) but manipulation needs fine-grained spatial features (contact points, precise object pose). Symptoms: features don't discriminate between success/failure states. Fix: use robotics-specific pre-training (R3M, Voltron), fine-tune last layers, or train a small task-specific head.
interview_answer: Pre-trained visual representations are a game-changer for sample-efficient robot learning. Instead of learning to see and act from scratch, we use pre-trained encoders (R3M, DINOv2, CLIP) and learn only the policy head. In practice: frozen pre-trained encoder + small MLP policy trained on 50-100 demos works surprisingly well for many manipulation tasks. The choice of pre-training matters: R3M (human video) and Voltron (robot video) capture manipulation-relevant features better than ImageNet-pretrained models. Key trade-off: frozen encoders are sample-efficient but may miss task-specific features; fine-tuning the last few layers helps when you have enough data.

title: Task Planning with LLMs for Robotics
definition: Using large language models to decompose high-level goals into executable sub-task sequences for robots. Hierarchical planning: $\text{LLM}(\text{goal}, \text{scene}) \rightarrow \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_T\}$ where each sub-task $s_i$ maps to a parameterized skill $\pi_{s_i}(a | o, \theta_i)$. Can be formalized as a PDDL-style planning problem where the LLM serves as both the domain modeler and the planner: given predicates $\mathcal{P}$, initial state $s_0$, and goal $g$, find action sequence $a_1, \ldots, a_T$ such that $s_T \models g$. Inner monologue and chain-of-thought improve multi-step reasoning.
intuition: Ask a robot to 'make a sandwich' and it needs to break that into: open the bread bag, take out two slices, get the peanut butter, open the jar, pick up a knife, spread, etc. LLMs excel at this common-sense task decomposition because they've seen millions of descriptions of everyday activities. The key is bridging the LLM's textual plan to the robot's physical skills — each sub-task must map to something the robot can actually do.
practical_example: SayCan + Inner Monologue pipeline: (1) VLM observes workspace, generates scene description. (2) LLM receives goal ('clean up the table') + scene description + available skills list. (3) LLM generates step-by-step plan: ['pick up the cup', 'place cup in sink', 'pick up the plate', ...]. (4) Each step is scored by affordance model $p(\text{feasible}|s_i, \text{state})$. (5) Highest-scoring feasible step is executed. (6) After execution, re-observe and re-plan (closed-loop). Error recovery: if a step fails, the LLM is prompted with the failure observation and re-plans.
failure_mode: Plan infeasibility: LLM generates physically impossible sequences (e.g., 'pick up the table' when the robot has a small gripper). Compounding errors: early step failure invalidates the rest of the plan but the system doesn't re-plan. Grounding mismatch: LLM refers to objects not present in the scene (hallucination). Symptoms: robot attempts impossible actions or gets stuck in loops. Fix: closed-loop re-planning after each step, affordance filtering, scene-state verification before each action, bounded re-planning attempts to avoid infinite loops.
interview_answer: LLM-based task planning bridges high-level reasoning and low-level robot execution. The key architecture: LLM as planner $\rightarrow$ affordance filter $\rightarrow$ skill library $\rightarrow$ low-level controller. This separates what to do (LLM) from how to do it (learned skills) and whether it's possible (affordance model). Critical design choices: (1) closed-loop replanning — always re-observe and re-plan after each step, (2) skill grounding — the LLM must only reference skills the robot actually has, (3) failure recovery — prompt the LLM with failure observations for adaptive replanning. The main limitation: LLMs don't have physics intuition, so they may propose dynamically infeasible plans. I always pair LLM planning with a feasibility checker.

title: In-Context Learning and Few-Shot Prompting for Robotics
definition: Leveraging a foundation model's ability to adapt to new tasks at inference time through carefully constructed prompts containing examples, without any gradient updates. For robotics: providing the model with $k$ demonstration examples $\{(o_i, a_i)\}_{i=1}^{k}$ in the prompt to condition behavior on a new task. Formally, the predicted action is $a^* = \arg\max_a P_\theta(a | o_{\text{query}}, \{(o_1, a_1), \ldots, (o_k, a_k)\})$. Extends to Code as Policies: LLM generates executable robot code from a few examples of the desired input-output mapping.
intuition: Instead of retraining the entire model for each new task, you show it a few examples and it figures out the pattern. Like showing a new employee three examples of how to fill out a form — they generalize to the fourth without reading the manual. For robots, this means you can teach new behaviors by demonstrating a handful of times and describing them in the prompt, rather than collecting thousands of demonstrations and fine-tuning.
practical_example: Code as Policies (Liang et al.): The LLM is prompted with 3-5 examples mapping natural language commands to Python robot API calls. Example prompt includes: 'pick up the red block' $\rightarrow$ `obj = detect('red block'); pick(obj)`, 'move the cup 10cm left' $\rightarrow$ `obj = detect('cup'); move(obj, dx=-0.1)`. At test time, novel instruction 'put the green bottle behind the box' $\rightarrow$ LLM generates: `bottle = detect('green bottle'); box = detect('box'); place(bottle, box.pos + [0, -0.15, 0])`. No fine-tuning needed — pure in-context learning.
failure_mode: Prompt sensitivity: small changes in example formatting or ordering cause drastically different outputs. Distribution shift: in-context examples from one environment don't transfer to visually different scenes. Brittle code generation: LLM generates syntactically correct but semantically wrong API calls (e.g., wrong coordinate frame, missing collision checks). Symptoms: works perfectly on demo-like scenarios, fails unpredictably on novel ones. Fix: use structured output schemas, validate generated code against a safety checker before execution, include negative examples ('do NOT do X'), and test with diverse prompt variations.
interview_answer: In-context learning is the fastest way to get foundation models to do new robot tasks — no training, just prompting. The two main patterns: (1) Code as Policies — LLM generates executable code from few-shot examples, great for spatial reasoning and composition; (2) VLA prompting — condition a vision-language-action model on demonstration videos/trajectories. The key advantage: adapt to new tasks in minutes, not hours of training. The key limitation: performance ceiling is lower than fine-tuning, and prompt engineering is fragile. In practice, I use in-context learning for rapid prototyping and task specification, then fine-tune if we need robust production performance. Always validate LLM-generated code in simulation before real execution.
